title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling Playbook & Benchmarking Suite
author: Asha Patel
content:
Overview

This document consolidates the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling decisions, profiling/playbook steps, benchmarking suite design, recent release notes, known issues, and operational runbooks. It is intended for runtime engineers, SREs, and performance-focused reviewers. Follow referenced runbooks for escalation and emergency rollback procedures.

1) Runtime architecture (high level)
\Intro: The runtime is a GPU-optimized inference engine designed for low-latency, high-throughput LLM serving. It combines a model execution layer, a scheduling layer, KV cache management, and a telemetry/observability agent. Key design goals: predictable tail latency, graceful degradation, cost-efficient batching, and transparent metrics for cost/latency tradeoffs.

Components:
- Request ingress: HTTP/gRPC handlers -> per-route policy evaluation (SLO, routing policy).
- Router: routes to hosted/dedicated/private pools and applies fallback rules.
- Scheduler: forms batches, assigns to GPU workers, enforces fairness and preemption.
- Executor: kernel selection, optimized attention, quantized execution paths.
- KV cache: sharded, per-model prefix cache with eviction policies.
- Telemetry: token-level timing, GPU utilization, NVML metrics, tracing (OpenTelemetry).

SLOs and target thresholds (system-wide defaults):
- P50 generation latency (single-token streaming): <= 15ms
- P95 latency (up to 256 tokens): <= 120ms
- P99 latency (up to 512 tokens): <= 400ms
- Throughput per GPU (50B quantized model): target 350 tok/s sustained
- GC/eviction windows: KV cache hot window >= 5 minutes by default
\Ownership and contact: runtime-core@redwood.com (primary), oncall: serving-runtime-sre rotation.
\2) Kernel selection & scheduling strategy
\Goals: choose kernel implementations and scheduling policies to maximize utilization while meeting per-request latency budgets.
\Key policies:
- Model-aware kernels: runtime maintains a Kernel Catalog indexed by model-size, sequence-length distribution, and quantization profile. When a model is loaded it registers preferred kernel implementations and fallbacks.
- Two-tier scheduling:
  1. Fast-path (low-latency): Form small batches up to 8 requests with max batch window 4ms. Reserved for routes with strict latency SLOs.
  2. Throughput-path (cost-efficient): Larger batching (adaptive up to max_batch_tokens) with window up to 20ms for non-SLO workloads.
- Priority queues: requests tagged with priority (critical, standard, background). Critical requests preempt throughput-path batches when latency budget is at risk. Preemption is cooperative: worker will finish current kernel op then reschedule.
- Fair share across customers: per-tenant tokens/sec limits and soft fairness at the scheduler level. Sudden spikes are shape-limited by token-leaky-bucket.
- Pre-warming and kernel warm caches: workers maintain a small MRU of last-used kernels and pre-compiled plans for the most common sequence lengths (16/32/64/128/256).
\Scheduler knobs (config table):
| parameter | meaning | default |
|---|---:|---|
| max_batch_tokens | max number of tokens combined in a batch | 4096 |
| latency_fastpath_ms | batch wait window for fast-path | 4 |
| latency_throughput_ms | batch wait window for throughput-path | 20 |
| max_batch_size | max requests in a batch | 64 |
| preemption_threshold_pct | percent of latency budget remaining to trigger preemption | 30 |
| kernel_cache_slots | number of precompiled kernels to keep per-worker | 16 |
\Kernel fallback order example:
1) FP16 custom-attention kernel (preferred for >8k tokens/sec)
2) INT8 quantized kernel (if model has quant profile)
3) Generic fused-attention kernel
4) CPU fallback for small/edge cases (very high latency; flow goes to fallback policy)
\3) Profiling playbook (how-to troubleshoot performance regressions)
\Purpose: a repeatable set of steps to identify source of regression (network, ingress, scheduler, kernel, GPU mem/clocking, KV cache).
\Preconditions: reproduceable load (use the benchmarking harness) and a stable commit roll-back point.
\Steps:
1. Reproduce workload locally or on a staging pool with the same model and sequence distribution. Use harness: ./bench/run_harness.sh --model MODEL --seq-dist seq_profile.json --qps TARGET
2. Collect end-to-end traces (OpenTelemetry) for 5–30 minutes covering at least 1000 requests.
3. Capture per-token timing from the telemetry UI (route -> model -> token timing heatmap).
4. On the affected worker(s), collect GPU metrics: nvmlmon --duration 60 --output /tmp/gpu-metrics.json and nsys profile -o /tmp/nsys_report --trace=nvtx,osrt --capture-range=cuda:kernel
5. Generate flamegraphs for CPU and GPU kernels (use profile_to_flame.sh). Compare against baseline.
6. Check kernel selection logs: /var/log/runtime/kernel-selection.log (timestamped). Look for fallbacks or frequent recompile events.
7. Inspect KV cache hit rate: /metrics -> runtime.kv_cache.hits and runtime.kv_cache.evictions. If hit rate < 70% consider resizing cache or increasing shard affinity.
8. If OOM or allocator failures observed, capture dmesg and coredump: sudo journalctl -u serving-runtime -n 500 and /var/crash/*; escalate to runtime-core.
9. Iterate: change one knob (e.g., reduce max_batch_size by 25%) and re-run step 1. Record results in the regression triage ticket.
\Quick commands (examples):
- Start profiling on a worker: sudo nsys profile -o /tmp/run$(date +%s) --trace=nvtx,cuda,osrt --capture-range=process:1 ./bin/serving-runtime --config /etc/serving/config.yaml
- Dump kernel catalog: curl -sS http://localhost:9090/internal/kernel-catalog | jq . > /tmp/kernel_catalog.json
- KV cache stats: curl -sS http://localhost:9090/metrics | grep runtime_kv_cache
\4) Benchmarking suite (design & how to run)
\Purpose: provide reproducible microbenchmarks and end-to-end workloads used for model onboarding, release validation, and capacity planning. Bench harness resides in: infra/benchmarks/serving-harness
\Workload types:
- Micro: single-worker perf tests (seq len sweep, batch size sweep, kernel comparison).
- Mixed: multi-worker mixed-size requests matching production distribution.
- Stress: high-concurrency token storms for prewarm and autoscaler validation.
\Benchmark config (example file fields):
| field | description | example |
|---|---:|---|
| model_variant | model name and quant profile | redwood-70b-int8 |
| seq_profile | json distribution of sequence lengths | seq_profile_2026_q1.json |
| qps | target queries per second | 200 |
| duration_s | benchmark length | 600 |
| concurrency | client-side concurrency | 80 |
| collect_profiles | whether to collect nsys profiles | true |
\Baseline benchmarks to store per-release:
- Latency vs throughput curves (p50/p95/p99) for sequences: 64, 128, 256, 512.
- GPU tokens/sec and efficiency (tokens/sec/Watt).
- Kernel selection heatmap (percent time spent per kernel).
\How to run a basic suite (CI job example):
1. Checkout infra/benchmarks/serving-harness and set TEST_POOL env to your staging pool.
2. ./ci/run_bench.py --config ci_configs/redwood-70b-int8.json --output /tmp/bench-results --collect_profiles
3. Upload results to benchdb: ./ci/upload_results.py /tmp/bench-results --project serving-runtime --tag nightly-$(date +%F)
4. Review generated dashboards: benchdb -> serving-runtime -> nightly -> comparison view.
\5) Release notes (recent changes impacting performance)
\Release 2026-11-20 (v2.14.0) - highlights:
- Introduced cooperative preemption to reduce P99 tails for latency-critical routes (median P99 improvement 22%).
- Kernel catalog extended with INT8-fused matmul path for 30B+ models. Expect 1.6x tokens/sec improvement on T4/GA102 class hardware when using INT8 profiles.
- Default latency_fastpath_ms reduced from 6ms to 4ms for faster decisions.
- Fixed regression where kernel recompile would occur on sequence-length cliff changes.
\Release 2026-09-02 (v2.12.3) - bugfixes:
- Resolved KV cache tombstone leak that caused eviction storms under heavy burst traffic.
- Memory allocator improvements to reduce transient OOMs when many small requests hit simultaneously.
\6) Known issues (as of last_updated)
\- Large-model cold start slow kernel selection: first 3–5 requests for new sequence lengths can see elevated latency due to JIT/plan generation. Mitigation: preload common sequence lengths with prewarm job: ./tools/prewarm_kernels.sh --model MODEL --seqs 16,32,64,128.
- INT8 precision drift in long prompts for specific model variants: certain quant profiles exhibit token-level probability shifts over very long context (>2048). Mitigation: use mixed-precision fallback for >=2048 contexts or apply model-specific calibration. Tracking: INC-2026-334.
- Metric spikes under autoscaler churn: autoscaler scale-up events can temporarily fragment kernel cache leading to small latency blips. Mitigation: stagger scale operations by pool slice and enable kernel cache warmup hooks in the autoscaler.
\7) Runtime runbooks (incident procedures)
\A) Incident: sustained P95 > SLO for a latency-critical route
1. Confirm: check dashboard (console -> routes -> SLO) and correlate with upstream (ingress) and worker metrics.
2. Identify scope: is it single worker, pool, or global? Use /internal/pool-status endpoint to locate anomaly.
3. If single worker: cordon worker and route traffic away: ./tools/cordon_worker.sh WORKER_ID && verify traffic drains.
4. If pool-wide: check autoscaler events and recent deploys. Roll back last runtime build if necessary.
5. Apply emergency mitigation: enforce strict fast-path (latency_fastpath_ms=2ms) and reduce max_batch_size to limit tail exposure.
6. Create incident ticket and assign to runtime-core and oncall SRE.
\B) Incident: GPU OOMs / memory allocation failures
1. Collect logs: sudo journalctl -u serving-runtime -o cat -n 1000 > /tmp/runtime.log; gather /var/crash.
2. Identify offending request patterns via traces.
3. If caused by large batch/window: lower max_batch_tokens and restart worker.
4. If caused by model change (new weight format), pin previous model variant and notify model-onboarding.
5. For persistent OOMs, offload to lower-memory footprint model variant (e.g., INT8) and open task for allocator heap tuning.
\C) Incident: KV cache thrash (evictions > 1000/min)
1. Check metrics runtime_kv_cache_evictions_total and hit rate.
2. Increase kernel_cache_slots and KV shard affinity for hot tenants.
3. If caused by tenant imbalance, apply tenant isolation policy: reserve cache slots by tenant priority.
\8) Team wiki and operational hygiene
\- Add a link to the runbook in the team wiki page: Confluence -> eng-serving-runtime -> runbooks. Keep runbook short and link back to this canonical doc for detailed procedures.
- Daily perf check: automated job posts P50/P95 trends to #runtime-alerts slack at 09:00 UTC. Any deviation > 20% creates a me ng channel with runtime-core and SRE.
- Post-mortem policy: every incident with P99 degradation > 2x baseline requires a blameless postmortem within 72 hours. Attach profiling artifacts and flamegraphs.
